statement: Let $f(x)=\\tfrac{\\mathrm{e}^{x}}{\\mathrm{e}^{x}+1}$. Show that $f$ is increasing, state its range, and find $f^{-1}(x)$.
solution: $f'(x)=\\tfrac{\\mathrm{e}^{x}(\\mathrm{e}^{x}+1)-\\mathrm{e}^{x}\\cdot\\mathrm{e}^{x}}{(\\mathrm{e}^{x}+1)^{2}}=\\tfrac{\\mathrm{e}^{x}}{(\\mathrm{e}^{x}+1)^{2}}>0$, so $f$ is increasing. As $x\\to-\\infty$, $f\\to0$; as $x\\to\\infty$, $f\\to1$; range $(0,1)$. For the inverse, set $y=\\tfrac{\\mathrm{e}^{x}}{\\mathrm{e}^{x}+1}\\Rightarrow y(\\mathrm{e}^{x}+1)=\\mathrm{e}^{x}\\Rightarrow \\mathrm{e}^{x}(1-y)=y\\Rightarrow x=\\ln\\tfrac{y}{1-y}$. So $f^{-1}(x)=\\ln\\tfrac{x}{1-x}$ (for $0<x<1$).
hints: Solve $y=f(x)$ for $x$ to get the inverse.
